596.title: By the mount and the book
596.hook: by the mount, and a book inscribed on open parchment (52:1–3)
596.howItsDone: Muslims handle the Qur'an with care: many perform ablution before touching the Arabic text, keep it on a high shelf, and say bismillah before reading; the Prophet's recitation of At-Tur in the sunset prayer is often followed by imams.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was 'ibadah, worship as wide as everything Allah loves. Your line: made for worship.

A young man from Mecca named Jubayr ibn Mut'im came to Medina after the battle of Badr, on business about prisoners. He wasn't a Muslim. At sunset he heard the Prophet ﷺ leading the prayer, reciting aloud. Years later he described the moment, and his words are in Sahih al-Bukhari: when the recitation reached certain verses, my heart nearly flew. The surah he heard was At-Tur, the Mount.

At-Tur, like Adh-Dhariyat, begins with oaths. Pickthall's translation: "By the Mount, And a Scripture inscribed On fine parchment unrolled." The commentators understand the Mount, at-Tur, as Mount Sinai, where Musa heard Allah speak. The Arabic tur means a mountain, and in the Qur'an it points again and again to that one. Then a book: kitabin mastur, written in lines, on raqqin manshur, parchment spread open. Raqq is fine, thin skin prepared for writing, kept for texts meant to last. Which book? Commentators differ. Some say the Torah given at that mountain. Some say the Qur'an. Some say the preserved tablet in heaven, or the records of deeds every person will see unrolled. The verse doesn't specify, and the scholars hold several views. What's clear is the pairing: a mountain and a page. A place where revelation happened, and the writing that carries it to people who weren't there. The oaths continue: by the frequented House, by the roof raised high, by the swelling sea. And they're answered: the punishment of your Lord will surely come. Jubayr's heart nearly flew a little later in the surah, at verses that ask: were they created out of nothing, or are they the creators? A question, not an argument. Reports say it was the first time faith settled in his heart, and he later became a Muslim. A recited page did that, in the half-light, to a man who came only for business.
screen: `AT-TUR: THE MOUNT OF MUSA.` · `RAQQ: PARCHMENT SPREAD OPEN.` · `WHICH BOOK? SEVERAL VIEWS.` · `A MOUNTAIN AND A PAGE.`

segments.voice: If there's a book you value near you, a Qur'an, a Bible, a book of poems, a family journal, bring it close; if not, picture one. Before you open it, notice its weight, the cover, the edges of the pages, then open it slowly, as if it were parchment that might tear, and read one line. If you pray, you can say bismillah before you open it.
At-Tur: the Mount, understood as Mount Sinai where Musa heard Allah speak, the oaths that open this surah alongside a book written in lines on parchment spread open. Today's word.
Your line: by the mount. A mountain stays put, but a page can travel far. Until tomorrow.

597.title: When the stars retreat
597.hook: glorify Him when you rise and at the retreat of the stars (52:48–49)
597.howItsDone: Many Muslims pray two short voluntary units before the obligatory dawn prayer, and say subhanallah, often thirty-three times, after prayers and in the early morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was At-Tur, the Mount, paired with a book on parchment spread open. Your line: by the mount.

At the very end of the night, the sky is still dark, but something has already shifted. The faint stars go first. Then the brighter ones, one by one, as if someone were walking through a house turning off lamps. Birds start before there's any light to speak of, and the whole change is over quickly. Surah At-Tur ends exactly there, at that hour, and tells the Prophet ﷺ what to do with it.
screen: `THE STARS GO OUT, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: The last two verses of At-Tur begin with comfort. Wait patiently for your Lord's decree, they tell the Prophet, for you are in Our sight. The Arabic is bi-a'yunina, literally within Our eyes: watched over, never out of view. Then the instruction, in Pickthall's translation: "And in the night-time also hymn His praise, and at the setting of the stars." Idbar an-nujum: the turning back of the stars, their retreat as dawn comes. Three times for glorifying, tasbih, are named across these two verses: when you rise, in the night, and as the stars withdraw. Commentators connected idbar an-nujum with the two short units of prayer before the dawn prayer, the sunnah of Fajr. A report attributed to Ibn 'Abbas says so, and other commentators followed him. The hadith tradition treats those two units with unusual tenderness. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says the two units before dawn are better than the world and everything in it. 'A'ishah reported, in Bukhari, that he was never more regular in any voluntary prayer than in those two. Notice the shape. It doesn't say glorify Him in the bright, busy middle of the day. It says, in effect: at the edges, when you've just risen and the night is letting go, the hours when nobody needs you yet. Subhanallah is the phrase of tasbih: glory be to Allah, far above every flaw. Said as the stars fade, it meets the day before the day starts asking things of you.

Tasbih: glorifying God, named three times at the edges of night and day in Surah At-Tur's last verses, as the stars withdraw. Today's word.
Your line: as the stars fade. The first minute can be praise, or simply stillness. That's day five hundred ninety-seven.

598.title: Not from desire
598.hook: by the star, your companion is not astray, nor does he speak from desire (53:1–3)
598.carry: you know better the affairs of your world
598.tomorrow: The lote tree of the boundary
598.howItsDone: Muslims cite 53:3–4 as a basis for following the Prophet's Sunnah alongside the Qur'an, and scholars of hadith built careful methods for recording and checking his words.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tasbih, praise at the edges of the day. Your line: as the stars fade.

A young man named 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr used to write down everything the Prophet ﷺ said. Every word. Some men of Quraysh told him to stop: he's a human being, they said, he speaks in anger and in good moods; why write it all? So 'Abdullah stopped, and went to ask. The Prophet pointed to his own mouth and told him to keep writing. Nothing comes out of this, he said, except truth. Today's surah has a verse behind that answer.

Surah An-Najm, the Star, the fifty-third, opens with one oath. Pickthall's translation: "By the Star when it setteth, Your comrade erreth not, nor is deceived; Nor doth he speak of (his own) desire." Which star? Commentators differ: the Pleiades, a falling star, any star at its setting. The oath is by something going down, out of sight, while what the surah defends stays. Then: your comrade, sahibukum. Not the Prophet or the Messenger, but your companion, the man who grew up among you; the verse speaks to people who knew him. Then the key line: wa ma yantiqu 'anil-hawa. Nor does he speak from desire. Hawa is the desire that pulls you along, the word from the day desire was read as a god. Here the surah says the one bringing the message isn't driven by it. The next verse: it is nothing but revelation revealed. How far does that reach? Scholars have discussed it carefully. It covers the Qur'an, first of all. Sunni scholarship has long held that his teaching in religious matters, the Sunnah, also rests on revelation in a broader sense, one reason hadith became a source of law. Scholars also point to a report where he gave an opinion in a worldly matter, how to pollinate date palms, and later said: you know better the affairs of your world. On this reading, the verse isn't a claim that he never had a personal view. It's a claim about the message: it isn't self-serving, and it isn't his wanting dressed up as revelation.
screen: `BY THE STAR AS IT SETS.` · `SAHIBUKUM: THE COMPANION YOU KNOW.` · `NOT FROM HAWA, BUT REVELATION.` · `HOW FAR IT REACHES: SCHOLARS WEIGH IT.`

segments.voice: Think of a conversation coming up today: advice you'll give, a recommendation, an opinion at work. Ask yourself honestly where your words might lean toward what you want, looking good, winning, getting your way, and choose one place to say what's true and useful for the other person, even if it gains you nothing. If you pray, you can ask for an honest tongue.
Hawa: the desire that pulls a person along; 53:3 says the Prophet does not speak from it, only revelation. Today's word.
Your line: you know better the affairs of your world. A small line about date palms, and a large one about trust. See you tomorrow.

599.title: The lote tree of the boundary
599.hook: he saw Jibril at the lote tree of the utmost boundary, near the garden (53:13–15)
599.howItsDone: Muslims remember the Isra' and Mi'raj, some with a yearly observance in the month of Rajab, retelling the journey to the lote tree and the gift of the five daily prayers; sidr leaves are still used in many places for washing the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hawa, the desire An-Najm says the Prophet doesn't speak from. Your line was you know better the affairs of your world.
screen: `YOU KNOW BETTER THE AFFAIRS OF YOUR WORLD.`

segments.voice: Sidr is a thorny tree of the Arabian desert, the lote tree: small leaves, small fruit, shade in a hard place. In a hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tells the women washing his daughter's body to use water and sidr, a practice that continues at funerals today. An ordinary desert tree. And the Qur'an puts one at the edge of everything, at a boundary commentators describe as the farthest point anything created can reach.
screen: `WATER AND SIDR FOR WASHING THE DEAD.`

segments.voice: Surah An-Najm describes two times the Prophet saw the angel Jibril in his true form. The first was on the horizon, near the beginning. The second, in Pickthall's translation: "And verily he saw him yet another time By the lote-tree of the utmost boundary, Nigh unto which is the Garden of Abode." Sidrat al-muntaha. Muntaha means the end point, the furthest limit. Commentators explain it as the place beyond which no created being passes, where the knowledge of creatures stops. They link this second sighting to the Night Journey and Ascension, the Isra' and Mi'raj, when the Prophet was taken through the heavens. 'A'ishah and Ibn Mas'ud both said, in reports in the two Sahihs, that what he saw at the tree was Jibril as he truly is; Ibn Mas'ud reported six hundred wings. The hadith of the Ascension in Bukhari describes the tree itself: fruits like great clay jars, leaves like elephants' ears, rivers flowing from its roots. Then something covered the tree, a covering the surah doesn't name, and commentators call it beyond description. And a short line: the sight did not swerve, nor did it go beyond. At the edge of everything, he didn't look away, and he didn't grab for more than he was shown. Notice the image. Not a palace or a throne at the boundary, but a tree, the kind that gives shade in hard places.
screen: `JIBRIL, SEEN A SECOND TIME.` · `SIDRAT AL-MUNTAHA: THE FARTHEST LIMIT.` · `FRUIT LIKE JARS, LEAVES LIKE EARS.` · `THE SIGHT DID NOT SWERVE.`

segments.voice: Sit at an edge, a doorstep, a window, the end of a street, or picture one, with inside on one side and outside on the other. Look steadily at what's in front of you, the way the verse describes: without swerving, and without reaching for more. If you pray, ask for that steadiness.
Muntaha: the end point, the furthest limit any created being can reach, marked by the lote tree where the Prophet saw Jibril again. Today's word.
Your line: the farthest tree. The edge of everything is marked by something that gives shade. Good to see you today.

600.title: Only what he strives for
600.hook: a person has only what he strives for, and his striving will be seen (53:39–40)
600.howItsDone: Pilgrims perform the sa'y, walking seven times between Safa and Marwah in memory of Hajar; Muslims also give charity and pray on behalf of parents who have died, as hadith describe.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Muntaha, the farthest limit, marked by a lote tree. Your line was the farthest tree.

Day six hundred. However those mornings came, with full attention, half-asleep, or pressing play just to keep the streak alive, they were somebody's effort. A milestone invites a tally: days, streaks, minutes. Surah An-Najm keeps a different kind. It's about what a person ends up holding at the end: not what they hoped for, not what they inherited, not what someone said about them. What they actually strove for, and nothing else.

Verses thirty-nine and forty, in Pickthall's translation: "And that man hath only that for which he maketh effort, And that his effort will be seen." The word is sa'y: striving, effort, going toward something on purpose. If you've followed the pilgrimage, you've met it. The sa'y is the walk, seven times, between the hills of Safa and Marwah, remembering Hajar running between them searching for water for her baby, Isma'il. Effort as a body moving toward what it needs. The verse sits in a passage the surah says was in the scrolls of Musa and of Ibrahim: no soul carries another's burden, and a person has only what they strive for. Two promises come out of it. Nobody can take your effort from you, or be credited with it in your place. And it will be seen, not necessarily by people. Seen. Scholars raise an honest question here. What about charity given for the dead, or prayers for a parent who's gone? Hadith in Bukhari and Muslim say such things do reach the dead. Scholars reconcile it in different ways. Some say a righteous child is part of the parent's own striving: a hadith in Muslim names a good child who prays for you among the three things that continue after death. Others say the verse sets the rule of justice, and Allah's generosity can add to it. Either way, in the verse's words, a person's effort is theirs, and it will be seen.

601.title: The moon split
601.hook: the Hour draws near and the moon is split (54:1)
601.howItsDone: Muslims recite Surah Al-Qamar and count the splitting of the moon among the Prophet's miracles; the Prophet recited it, with Surah Qaf, in the Eid prayers, and many imams still do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sa'y, effort toward what you need, and your line, only what you strive for.

A clear night at Mina, just outside Mecca. The moon over the mountains. A group of men from Quraysh have come to the Prophet ﷺ with a challenge: show us a sign. What happened next is reported by several Companions, in the most trusted hadith collections, and it gave the fifty-fourth surah its name: Al-Qamar, the Moon. Its first verse holds two things that don't obviously belong together: the end of time, and a moon.
screen: `THE END OF TIME, AND A MOON.`

segments.voice: Pickthall: "The hour drew nigh and the moon was rent in twain." Iqtarabat as-sa'ah: the Hour has come near. Wanshaqqa al-qamar: and the moon split. In Sahih al-Bukhari, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud says he was there. The moon split in two, one part over the mountain and one beyond it, and the Prophet said: bear witness. Anas ibn Malik reports that the Meccans had asked for a sign, and they were shown this. Most classical scholars read the verse this way, as an event in the Prophet's lifetime. A minority read the past tense as a vivid way of describing something certain to come with the Hour. Verse two gives the reaction: if they see a sign, they turn away and say, a magic that keeps going. The surah's point isn't astronomy. It's the gap between seeing and accepting: people asked for a sign, saw one, and found a word to explain it away. Why put the moon next to the Hour? Commentators note that the Hour's nearness runs through these late surahs. The Prophet once held up two fingers side by side and said: I and the Hour were sent like these two. The split moon is presented as an early crack in the ordinary, a sign the world's order isn't permanent. One honest note. You may see claims online that space agencies photographed proof of the split. No such confirmation exists, and the tradition never rested on one. It rests on the reports of people who said they saw it.
screen: `IBN MAS'UD: BEAR WITNESS.` · `MOST SAY: AN EVENT IN HIS LIFETIME.` · `THEY SAW A SIGN AND CALLED IT MAGIC.` · `A CRACK IN THE ORDINARY.`

segments.voice: Find the moon tonight, whatever its phase, or picture the last one you remember. Look long enough for it to stop being familiar: a stone hanging in nothing, lit by a sun you can't see. If you pray, you can say subhanallah.
Al-Qamar, the Moon, the surah named for the night the moon split in two before men who asked for a sign. Today's word.
Your line: the hour draws near. The moon is still up there, a reminder that time moves. Day six hundred one, done.

602.title: Easy to remember
602.hook: We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; is there any who will remember (54:17)
602.carry: is there any who will remember?
602.howItsDone: Many Muslims memorize short surahs as children for the daily prayers, and some memorize the whole Qur'an with a teacher who listens line by line; a person who has done so is called a hafiz.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Surah Al-Qamar opened with the moon split in two, and your line was the hour draws near. Today closes the week.

Someone reads you a phone number once. A minute later it's gone. But the chorus of a song you haven't heard in ten years is still there, every word, back the moment the first note plays. Some words stick. Surah fifty-four, the Moon, tells one hard story after another: Nuh and the flood, the people of 'Ad and the wind, Thamud and the she-camel, the people of Lut. And between the stories, like a chorus, one line keeps coming back. It's about remembering, and it ends with a question.

Verse seventeen. Pickthall: "And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?" The line returns, almost word for word, in verses twenty-two, thirty-two and forty: four times, each after a story closes. The Arabic for we have made it easy is yassarna, from the root y-s-r, ease. And remembering is dhikr, the remembrance this path has met so often. Classical commentators read the verse two ways at once. Easy to remember: the Qur'an is easy to hold in memory. And easy for remembrance: easy to take a reminder from. The first reading is lived out. Children and adults memorize the entire book, and someone who has done it is called a hafiz, a keeper or guardian of it. Some do it before Arabic is their everyday language, with a teacher listening line by line. But the verse doesn't stop at the ease. It ends on a question: fa hal min muddakir, so is there anyone who will remember? The ease is offered; someone has to pick it up. And a hadith in Bukhari adds a kindness for those who find it hard. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said the one skilled in the Qur'an will be with the noble scribes, and the one who struggles, reciting with difficulty, has a double reward. So the question isn't only for the gifted. It's put to anyone with one verse they could learn.
screen: `FOUR TIMES IN ONE SURAH.` · `Y-S-R: WE MADE IT EASY.` · `A HAFIZ KEEPS THE WHOLE BOOK.` · `A DOUBLE REWARD FOR THE ONE WHO STRUGGLES.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim, take a verse you half-know, maybe the opening of Surah Al-Ikhlas, and say it slowly, again and again, until it holds without looking. If that isn't yours, say today's line on the out-breath a few times: is there any that remembereth? Then stop, and see whether it stays with you in the quiet.
Dhikr: remembrance, the word behind Surah Al-Qamar's chorus that the Qur'an was made easy to hold onto, asking four times who will take it up. Today's word.
Your line: is there any who will remember? The week climbed from the Mount and the fading stars, through the Star and its lote tree, to the split moon and today's chorus. See you tomorrow.
